utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Are there any matters to raise before we have evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you and good morning. Mr. President, we would like to withdraw our request to have Exhibit MFI D1051 admitted, the statement of Senaid Memic. We decided that after the point raised by the Chamber, it's not in our interests to ask that that statement be admitted at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Secondly, we would like to discuss, before General Smith comes in, the situation concerning Rule 70. And I was wondering if we might go into private session to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we postponed as long as possible the questions about the Vrbanja Bridge, that is the subject of the Rule 70 condition. And Mr. Tieger has informed me, and he can speak for himself, that the UN has not yet made a final decision as to whether or not they are going to insist upon that condition, but we feel this is a matter that ought to be addressed in the way of somehow practice and precedent of the Chamber, that when there's a Rule 70 condition, we think, first of all, there ought to be advance notice to the parties and the Chamber well before the witness testifies, that there is a Rule 70 condition that is being asserted, so that we could try to clear all the problems in advance of the testimony of the witness, rather than having testimony in private session that may later be -- come into the public session, when there's no real interest in this testimony anymore. So we would appreciate if the Chamber might consider making some kind of order to the Prosecution in the future that part of its notifications about the witnesses should include any Rule 70 conditions. Secondly, with respect to this particular condition, we think that it's advisable that the Chamber have the provider be more accountable for conditions which seem, on their face, to be unreasonable, in the sense that General Smith has given this very testimony in public session in the Dragomir Milosevic case, and his testimony was admitted as a public exhibit in the Momcilo Perisic case. And so I would ask that you order that there be an oral hearing on Friday, at 10.00, at which the representative of the United Nations would appear before the Chamber to explain why the need -- there is a need for the Rule 70 condition of General Smith, and then you can decide afterwards whether the remedy of excluding all or part of his testimony might be applicable. But I think it's necessary to have some accountability for these providers in circumstances such as this, where the condition appears to be unreasonable. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mean after we will have received all of General Smith's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't propose holding up his evidence, but I would like to keep -- while the matter is still fresh, I'd like to keep some pressure so that the matter can be resolved by the end of the week. Otherwise, it's liable to linger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to respond, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, briefly. With respect to Mr. Robinson's point that there ought to be advance notice to the parties, I trust that the Court will recall that the genesis of this problem is that, notwithstanding the one-year advance notice provided by the Prosecution to the Defence - I believe the Court saw that notification - this matter was not raised until the witness came to court. Once it was raised by the Defence, the Prosecution acted with the utmost alacrity to contact the UN, provide all the relevant materials, stress the urgency, and push for reconsideration again, as we had before. But in light of these circumstances, with the utmost haste. Unfortunately, three working days is insufficient to work through that process, although we had hoped that the matter might be resolved today. But to suggest that somehow there was no notice here, by posing this proposed condition in this manner, I think, is quite unfair under the circumstances. Secondly, with respect to the proposed hearing, I think the Court has already alluded to the Tribunal's jurisprudence on this matter, the fact that the providers are not required to justify their conditions. In any event, the reality of the situation, as I've advised the Court, is that the UN has been contacted. I am optimistic that we will be hearing back shortly. Everyone has moved forward on this, under these circumstances, with the utmost haste. And to suggest that some further procedural developments and obligations are necessary here, I think, is unfounded and inappropriate, and the reality of the matter is this is a fairly commonplace situation, in terms of hearing a matter in private session. We have reason to hope that we will, in short order, be able to transform that into public session, as I've advised Mr. Robinson. In any event, even if not, it neither justifies the attention that this issue has generated, nor any special hearing to address a matter that the providers are not required to address or justify. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question for you. You mentioned that there was one-year advance notice provided by the Prosecution to the Defence in this regard. So the Defence was informed about that Rule 70 condition a year ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe I'm obtuse, but when the notice that we received in February of 2010 said that we were not to disclose to anyone else paragraph 134 of the statement of Rupert Smith, and that statement never was used, it was not an exhibit, a further amalgamated statement was provided which didn't have any conditions. All of the underlying documents concerning this event were provided to us without any Rule 70 conditions, and I never made the connection between the 2010 February restriction on one paragraph and a statement that was not going to be used to a condition based on the testimony of the -- the live testimony of the witness, and maybe that's my fault. But if there is going to be notice, perhaps it could be a little bit more clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would expect the messages in the future to be a bit clearer between the parties, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will, as always, endeavour to make those messages as clear as possible. However, as the Court is aware, that referred to a specific paragraph. It was the paragraph in the amalgamated statement. We looked at it the other day. We've gone through this discussion before, and as the Court noted previously, Mr. Robinson's request is a belated one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And as regards -- with respect to the hearing, you suggested that at this moment we find it a bit premature and unnecessary to set a date for hearing at this moment. Having said that, we'll go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just I wanted to raise two matters with the Court. The first is that with respect to a matter the Court inquired about yesterday, that is, the scheduling date for Mr. Banbury, we've heard back, and the 15th of March is satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Secondly, in light of the current schedule and General Smith's return, it is clear that we will not get to the testimony of Mr. Music this week, so he will not be appearing this week. I may also note that depending on our schedule for the rest of the week, with the various uncertainties of which the Court is aware with certain -- the length of testimony and witnesses appearing, there is an issue about whether or not Mr. Mujkic will be testifying this week as well. So Mr. Music will not be appearing, and in light of the current schedule or anticipated schedule, we'll have to see about Mr. Mujkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. There's one further matter to raise on the part of the Chamber. The Chamber has been requested by the Defence to lift the confidentiality of all the filings that pertain to Mr. Berko Zecevic, of which the Prosecution is in agreement. Mr. Zecevic is listed as a witness for the Prosecution and is the subject of a subpoena issued by this Chamber on 20th January 2011. The Chamber subsequently issued an order, in lieu of indictment, and warrant of arrest for Mr. Zecevic, in light of his failure to give testimony on the date specified in the subpoena. The Chamber is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice for the filings in relation to this matter to now be made public, and we'll order the Registry to do so, with the exception of certain supporting medical documentation which shall remain under seal. The Chamber will communicate to the Registry, via its Legal Officer, the precise documents which should now be reclassified as public documents. Let us bring in the witness. Just for your information, last evening -- yesterday, the Chamber already authorised the Tribunal's press office to confirm the existence of the order, in lieu of indictment, and the arrest warrant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, General. We appreciate your kindness to come back to the Tribunal again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I hope we'll be able to finish your evidence during the course of today, hopefully before 12.30, the second session. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Good morning to all. Good morning, General. Thank you, on behalf of the Defence again, for having coming back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like us to complete the topic that remained unfinished last time. Do you agree with the fact that President Milosevic, on the 4th of August, 1994, severed all ties with us and imposed sanctions against us on the Drina?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the details of that. I remember that there was some public severance of relations in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this isolation was widely orchestrated and that certain representatives of the international community had insisted on it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my knowledge is based, at the time of 1994, on being in London. And I remember the matter being discussed, but to the -- but the absolute details of it and the extent of the decisions made, as opposed to the conversations being held, I don't recall the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that President Carter partly broke that isolation down by coming in December 1994? After that, we concluded the so-called Carter Cease-Fire, a four-month cease-fire, and in the meantime you arrived in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, President Carter was there at the very end of 1994, and the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement was signed thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that right after your arrival in February 1995, at the initiative of Anthony Lake and Richard Holbrooke, yet again the isolation of the leadership in Pale of Republika Srpska, especially of Radovan Karadzic, was reinforced?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that specifically. I can -- nor do I remember the subject of isolation being a particular issue discussed with me at all until sometime, I think, in March of 1995, or maybe it was April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was communicated to you at that point in time, what was the position to be taken vis-a-vis the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't communicated to me as any instruction at all. I had no direction, in terms of isolation, whatsoever, and nor did I act in that way. I was aware that this was an idea that was being considered, as I said, in 1994, although exactly when that was being discussed, I can't recall. And it became -- I became aware of it being discussed again. It was discussed in my presence, rather than with me, as it were, as instructions to me or anything like that, probably in April - now I'm thinking about it more carefully - when the Contact Group or members of the Contact Group visited or tried to visit Sarajevo. But this is supposition. I have very little clear memory of that, if you like, contextual discussion with me at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that when you testified in General Perisic's case, on page -- just a moment, please. I beg your pardon -- that you said that people did not know who was speaking on behalf of the Bosnian Serbs? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There was about to be a page reference, but I don't believe I ever heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the page number, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I'll try to find it now. Just a moment. This would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You testified in the Perisic case, that is, on the 20th of May, 2009, page 6386. You said then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you still remember the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's a direct quote that I say I don't know, and I think this is a piece of evidence that's concerning March of 1995 and a discussion with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. It wasn't March; it was August of 1995, and a conversation with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- or, rather, can you tell us who Aleksandar Ivanko was?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aleksandar Ivanko was one of my spokesmen. He was the UN spokesman, as opposed to the military spokesman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in the summer of 1995, Mr. Ivanko said at a press conference that the political leadership of the Bosnian Serbs does not have sufficient influence on the ground and that they would not communicate with them anymore, that they don't have leverage on the events? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it specifically, no. And when did he say it in the summer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we looked for those conferences, but it was in the summer of 1995. And I believe that he had to have permission to state something like that. Right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no. I would want to know when in -- about what is he talking, to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this will do. If you don't know, you don't know. We're going to get the document, itself. However, according to my notes, this was in the summer of 1995. It was a press conference when he stated that the United Nations would not have much to do with the political leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, General: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Still trying to find the reference in the Perisic testimony. I've now scoured 6386 more than once, and there's -- that reference doesn't appear there. If the Defence could check that and provide the correct page number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I hope the Defence would be able to give you a reference later on. In the meantime, let's continue. Where are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you remember that - actually, just a moment, please - that this was a rather wide undertaking, to have the leadership isolated and to stop ending communication with the leadership, and to find other solutions through President Milosevic for resolving the situation in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it like that, no. From my point of view, in the job I was doing in 1995, I was given no direction - in fact, on the contrary, encouragement to deal with the Bosnian Serb leadership. Being on the military side, my emphasis lay with the military, but not exclusively. And the moment my new Civil Affairs -- chief of Civil Affairs - I've forgotten his proper title, but he was called Mr. Pedaway [phoen] - arrived in August, he went straight up to Pale to talk to the leadership in that place. What I -- I entirely agree that outside of my little world, if you like, there was this policy of dealing with Mr. Milosevic. To what extent that was, other than it had a label, in my mind, called "Isolation," I do not know to the degree to which it was being practiced to any great -- to any great degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll help you, so that we both jog our memory, with Carl Bildt's book and Ambassador Holbrooke's book. I'm sorry, that was reference was -- it had to do with the Milosevic case, actually, the Slobodan Milosevic case, October 2003. And as for Dragomir Milosevic, on the 27th of March, 2007. It's an exhibit there, P344. It says there that you said that you were trying to establish who was speaking on behalf of the Bosnian Serbs, since during June, July and part of August: [In English] "The senior level arrangements for the Bosnian Serbs in Pale were under pressure. The relations between Mladic and Karadzic was unclear." [Interpretation] Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, and I'm not clear which of those two cases you're quoting from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Say from Milosevic, the 7th of March, 2007. The page is 3334. As for President Milosevic, statement paragraph 104.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you like to put the specific question, why don't you show the passage to the general, and let us see whether he confirms.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just wanted to get a yes-or-no answer. It's all the same. I just wanted the general to give a yes-or-no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the summer of 1995, June, July and part of August, the general did not know who was speaking on behalf of the Bosnian Serbs, As he confirmed in his statement - just a moment, please - when he testified in the case against President Milosevic and the case against General Milosevic. Can you remember that? You said you were confused by all this, Don't talk to this person, Don't talk to that person, and, Milosevic was supposed to speak on behalf of us? ^

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, I've been looking through the transcripts as we've been speaking. I didn't see any reference to the word "confused." Secondly, I don't see, if the witness is being confronted with his prior statement, why he has to remember it, why it can't be cited to him properly and read to him in context. So I've tracked down one of the references in the original reference that Mr. Karadzic made in the Perisic case, and it's not quite the same comment posed, and now I see, in the Dragomir Milosevic case, what the witness talks about is also a bit different, in context, to what's being presented to him. And if he's going to be asked about what he said and asked to comment on it, I think he should be given a fair opportunity to know what that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By adding your statement or comments, you make your question very complicated. I think by now, General, I take it the General has understood the question. I wonder whether you can answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure I would -- my memory is this: that I was always searching to understand who was speaking for the Bosnian Serbs. There was this relationship between General Mladic and Dr. Karadzic, and it -- there was -- I was trying to understand it, trying to understand who was speaking for who and in what circumstances throughout that summer, and I think those remarks and those statements are situated within the context of that understanding as being discussed in those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at a meeting -- at two meetings that you described, secret meetings, private, if I can call them that, that I said to you that as regards matters pertaining to safe passage, convoys, et cetera, that you should talk to my commanders; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to remember that was your -- what you told me to do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that I was the political leader, the state leader in the civilian sphere, and that I had to leave expert matters to my army, as is done in any country?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that quite an effort was made to sow discord between the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs and the military commands and that quite a bit was done in order to turn Mladic against us? Milosevic worked on that, and all international factors as well. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember it as you describe it. I remember there was discord. I had no knowledge of the specific details, but as I think I've reported already, that one was clear that all was not always in agreement. But I don't recall efforts to make it worse, certainly not by UNPROFOR or the UN.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 1D3201.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While I'm looking for that: Can you tell us, General, what is SEAD, what does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suppression of Enemy Air Defences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least it did in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that that was the basis for taking a position vis-a-vis the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't understand the question. I certainly don't remember it as a position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 69. It's different in electronic form, but it's page 69 of this document. I mean, in the book itself, page 69. Page 69 in the book, itself. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "SEAD campaigns - suppression of enemy air defence - was necessary for a number of days and would preferably have to encompass the whole of Bosnia." [Interpretation] You can all have a look at this. It is based on the guide-lines of the London Conference. General, who was this supposed enemy in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just finishing reading. What is the -- is this prior the London Conference or after? What is the page -- can I see the page before?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, let us place this in context. Who convened the London Conference, and who are the participants?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still not clear if the decisions had been ... This page 68 is about the London Conference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you see the next page, next paragraph on page 69, it refers to "sometime in July." Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Without going back through all the pages, this looks like a discussion of either what was going on in the background of the London Conference or just prior to the London Conference, but I'm not certain. However, to answer the question: The use of the phrase "SEAD," or the SEAD as it gets spelled, or pronounced, rather, is a way of describing the precursor phase of an air action. It -- you have to do this before you can get in and attack the targets you've actually been sent to attack, and so it this -- you might make a plan, and this precursor phase would appear in it. Whether you had decided to carry out -- execute the plan or not, you would still have worked out your suppression of air defences operation that would precede and be the necessary enabling objectives to carry out the actual act. So if you were told to carry out a -- to make a plan to conduct such an air operation against whomsoever, you would have an SEAD phase in it of some description, and that would be why that was being discussed at that stage, I suspect. And since these were all in defence of and to reimpose the exclusion zones around the enclaves, then the Bosnian Serbs would -- the assumption would be that the Bosnian Serbs were attacking the -- those enclaves, and, therefore, it would be the air defences -- the Bosnian Serb air defences that one was seeking to attack.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please look at page 67, two pages back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind to focus on this page, where there is an explanation of the context of the London Conference, and could you tell us who had convened the London Conference, and what was the subject to be discussed, and what was the goal and the objective of the conference?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'd be concerned, the London Conference was convened by the United Kingdom, and the underpinning events that led to it was the collapse of the Srebrenica pocket and all that followed thereafter. And the intention was that this was not to happen in Gorazde, in the first instance, and this was where a British battalion was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- do you remember, rather, what Operations Plan 40104 was? What did that refer to?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what that plan was or whose it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let me remind you. On Wednesday, the 28th of June, the NATO Council in Brussels decided to officially approve Operations Plan 04104 [as interpreted], which envisaged mass ground invasion of Bosnia, allegedly to provide for the withdrawal of UN forces. Did you know about that? And also there's mention there of the recently Rapid Reaction Forces. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember the Rapid Reaction Force, and I can remember that there was a contingency plan, the details of which I did not know, held by NATO for the extraction of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move back to page 64, please, two pages back -- three pages back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the last sentence in paragraph 1: [In English] "To use Mladic to undermine Karadzic was part of our efforts. And the Sarajevo leadership was aware of these intentions of ours." [Interpretation] Therefore, in co-operation with the Muslim leadership, efforts were being made to turn Mladic against Karadzic. Is this what Ambassador Bildt is saying here?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now look at the last paragraph, which refers to you and your future contacts with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in relation to the last question and answer, you asked the general whether it is what is written there, and he confirmed. It leads us nowhere, unless you hear his answers from the general, what Ambassador Bildt wrote in his book has nothing to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Smith attended meetings with President Milosevic, Carl Bildt and Mr. Holbrooke on occasion where they were working on bringing -- or toppling the authorities in Pale. These things were happening at the meetings with General Milosevic -- with President Milosevic. I don't know if the general paid attention to that. And he did confirm that he attended the meetings on the 14th and 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar or are you not familiar with these efforts to turn the military leadership against the state leadership, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not conscious that there was a deliberate process of turning the Bosnian Serb military against the Bosnian Serb political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you present in the meetings in which President Milosevic made promises and made predictions of the demise of the authorities in Pale?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that in the meetings that occurred that I was there, when Mladic was there, and Ambassador Bildt and President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now move to page 81, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look from paragraph 2 downwards, where it says that during the Croatian offensive, he wanted to meet Milosevic, together with Pauline Neville-Jones, Alain Dejammet, and so on and so forth. He was under pressure to say whether he could really deliver Pale. Now, look at the next passage. Do you remember that after the fall of Krajina -- do you see this passage where it says: [In English] "Pale was in a state of --"

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember that at that time, President Milosevic wrote a letter to President Izetbegovic and General Mladic: [In English] "The letter was a double insult of Karadzic, first by addressing Izetbegovic as President as president, and then by addressing the letter to Mladic, rather than to him. In Pale, it was considered quite rightly that this was a plot designed to isolate, marginalise and basically eliminate the existing Bosnian Serb leadership." [Interpretation] Did you, yourself, feel and did you know that that was the attitude that was taken vis-a-vis the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it as starkly explained in the paragraph you've asked me to read. My own memory of that period is one in which I'm conscious that the Bosnian Serbs are -- have now moved on to the back foot because of the Croatian offensive and have a great deal of troubles of their own. And you've -- and we've already seen in evidence this meeting in Mrkonjic Grad, where I'm trying to find out what's happening and establish the degree of humanitarian aid and so forth that is required of UNPROFOR for the people expelled from the Krajinas. I am not conscious of and have no part to play in any of this -- of the events that are described in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at this page? General, do you remember when you speak about humanitarian needs, there were huge influx of refugees coming into Krajina and Republika Srpska at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were coming from the Krajinas, weren't they? But, yes, I remember there was a large refugee problem, in the thousands, of people moving out of the Krajinas and into Bosnia-Herzegovina, some of whom were moving on into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a small suggestion. It may be helpful in posing questions on this topic to distinguish between the Croatian Krajina and the Bosnian Krajina. That may eliminate answers that appear to be -- well, to not make sense.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this suggestion from my learned friend Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we are talking about the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which was part of the AVNOJ Croatia. It came under attack in early August, and there were hundreds of thousands of people expelled from there. General, is that true?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the total figure. I think it was in excess of 100.000 expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I draw your attention to the beginning, where it says that the success of this plot, as Mr. Bildt calls it, the plot to isolate and remove the Bosnian Serb leadership from power, so I'm talking about the 4th of August and the dismissal of Mladic. Can you see this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, if we are not going to admit this into evidence, then I would like to read what is written here. If this is admissible, then I am reluctant to call Mr. Bildt to come here and appear as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you specifically put it to the witness. If necessary, you can read out the relevant passage. At this moment, I haven't discussed it with my colleagues, but speaking for myself, I don't think this is something admissible without having to hear from Mr. Bildt. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's -- the point has now been made, and the game is now revealed. It's an effort to circumvent the need to call Mr. Bildt by reading out passages of his book, asking the witness to do nothing more than to affirm that that's what's written there. And as the Court has previously noted, that's not an appropriate strategem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you are entitled to put questions, if necessary reading out passages from the book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. There's no game being played. I am just trying to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 reads. "Croat army made its pincer movement from both Croatia and Bosnia towards Knin. Karadzic, on 4 August, summarily fired Mladic, accusing him both of failing to defend key Serb areas properly and of having had unauthorised contacts with Stoltenberg and myself. Thus, Karadzic triggered an acute confrontation between the political and military leadership in the most desperate of situations. It seemed totally irrational, and, after a week of turmoil, Karadzic had to retreat and accept that Mladic would remain as the military commander." [Interpretation] Do you recall this crisis?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the specific thing of you writing a letter. I may never have known it had occurred. I do remember there was reports of this tension between the political and military leaderships, but this had been going on during the summer, and I was continuing to try and understand who was in charge of what and who was speaking for the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was a crucial event, and I am surprised that you don't remember it. There's reference here to my open letter to President Milosevic, which is in the next passage, and it reads: [In English] "Morale in the Republika Srpska was now at rock bottom. Eventually, more than 200.000 refugees would pass through Banja Luka and Brcko on their way to some sort of safety in Serbia, and there were rumours all over the place of secret deals, arrangements and plans giving up different territories. Karadzic wrote a public letter accusing Milosevic of a betrayal of Serb interest." [Interpretation] What I'm asking you now, sir, is whether you were aware or whether you knew that a lot of things had been done behind my back, starting from the London Conference, while, on the other hand, I was requested to honour the agreements that I was not party to.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of things in those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you learn anything about that later?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the way you posed that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Sir, are you aware that the issue of air-strikes against the Serbs was largely an issue that had to do with internal political circumstances in NATO member countries and that it had a lot to do with the credibility of the alliance, itself?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. That was not -- and it isn't my understanding at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since this is not being admitted, I would just like us to look at what Holbrooke says in his book about this topic. So he's talking about the credibility of NATO and the need to launch air-strikes against the Serbs, and to flex the muscle, because the credibility of NATO was at stake. I'm going to read this: [In English] "Bosnia will be the key test for American policy in Europe. We must, therefore, succeed in whether we attempt. The administration cannot afford to begin with either an international disaster or quagmire. Despite the difficulties and risks involved, I believe that inaction or a continuation of the Bush policy in Bosnia by the Clinton Administration is the least desirable course. Continued inaction carried long-term risk which could be disruptive to US-European relations, weaken NATO, increase tensions in Greece and Turkey, and cause havoc with Moscow."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, how were we to adjust our behaviour and conduct, because there was so many things against us and there was so many people pulling strings?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I -- I just don't know how to answer your question against the purposes of this court. I am sitting in my headquarters in Sarajevo. I am not an American, I am not part of the American policy-making, and I'm certainly not the late Mr. Richard Holbrooke. And the actions of the Bosnian Serbs were theirs to choose. It wasn't for me to dictate them or -- mine was to react in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, my question is: Did air-strikes depend exclusively on our conduct or did it have to do with something with internal policies and the credibility of NATO? I believe that there was a larger picture there, it wasn't just the matter of a small Serbian nation of, actually, 1.5 million Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer a question about your beliefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did these factors play any roles? You were the commander in Bosnia. Did you have an obligation to take that into account, because you, yourself, said on several occasions that you had close ties with the NATO?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have to take the making of policy and the decisions above me into account in the actions that I did. I had to understand their background and so forth, perhaps. But in these circumstances and that August, the decisions made in the London Conference had been made, they were quite clear, and I was confident that their import had been communicated to you, amongst others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in your talks with the key players, Annan; Admiral Smith, Leighton Smith; Akashi; Holbrooke and the others, was there any indication that there is something larger and more important at stake than the fate of the Bosnian Serbs? Did you discuss any of these matters?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The few discussions that occurred and were either to do, in the case of Admiral Leighton Smith, with the contingency planning we were conducting, and we've discussed already, I don't recall a conversation with Mr. Akashi, although I'm sure one happened in that August. And with Holbrooke and his team, it was -- there were -- I think he visited Sarajevo twice in that time, and they were -- I was given the most general of indications of what his negotiations -- how his negotiations were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's why it is so important to know who convened the London Conference, who took part in it, and what was to be achieved by the London Conference. Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you who convened it in -- that I think convened it, and that was the United Kingdom government. I think every single troop-contributing nation was present. And as far as I was concerned, it was all to do with the establishing a -- this change in the exclusion zone and safe area regime, for want of a name for it, that the decision as to whether there had been an attack on a safe area was now to lie with the military and not with the political chain of command. The keys to initiate air attacks were put in the hands of the military commanders, not the political -- the SRSG. They, after May, had been held by the Secretary-General, himself, from the point of view of NATO -- I beg your pardon, from the point of view of the UN. And the -- and the decision was that if bombing was initiated, this, if I remember the words correctly, would be continuous and disproportionate until the attack stopped and the exclusion zones were re-established, or something to that effect, and that these senior officers would be sent off to explain this to the parties concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for this information as well, that a disproportionate attack was decided on. Do you agree that Lieutenant-Colonel -- Lieutenant General Michael Ryan set the targets for that bombing months before a reason or pretext actually came up? This is Holbrooke's book, planned by Admiral Smith, page 103: [In English] "... planned by Admiral Smith and his brilliant air force commander, Lieutenant General Michael E. Ryan. The targets had been picked months in advance." [Interpretation] Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they'd been picked. They may have collected information, identified potential targets, but I don't think they'd been picked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do we agree that one air-strike took place in the absence of General Janvier, another one in the absence of the Secretary-General, and it was Kofi Annan who played a significant role?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about. Which air-strike?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of May, the first one. You said yourself, and you confirmed in your book, that General Janvier was on leave at the time when you availed yourself of the opportunity to turn the key, as it were, in order to start the bombing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, General: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to give as much latitude as possible, but I think we've gone beyond the outskirts of relevance and are no longer even remotely illuminating the issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. How is this last question relevant to your case, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, this has to do with side-stepping the people of top responsibility, the first echelon. And it is the second echelon that makes the decisions, and we have testimony to that effect in the book of the late Holbrooke, and it says here that Annan got the job of Secretary-General because he supported the bombing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Side-stepping that allegedly took place on the part of NATO, or whatever country, is relevant to your case how? Move on to another topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And, incidentally, Dr. Karadzic, you refer to the testimony in the book of the late Richard Holbrooke. What Mr. Holbrooke put in his book is not testimony, and it's certainly not testimony before this Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is testimony by a direct participant. I believe that the relevance lies in the fact that there is nothing we could have done in order to affect the developments that were underway. We were but a small toy in the hands of the big players. We have a witness here now who was on the ground and who was supposed to carry out, on the ground, something that had been planned at much higher levels. That is the relevance. However, we're going to move on to another topic. Can we just have 23210 for a moment -- 32390.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is marked for identification as MFI D987.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, please, would you focus on this conversation of mine with General Milovanovic on the 25th of September, when that first bombing took place. And I'm going to read this out. This is a copy of the conversation between Radovan Karadzic and General Milovanovic, and then this is a convention -- "Akashi has been chasing me all day. I didn't want to call him, but now I manage." It says: "Please, can you, over the next few minutes, try to do something? Is it so difficult to return those four weapons, some four weapons? Nikola is here as well. I said many things to him. He says that he was with Mladic and with you, that he was in contact with you and Mladic. Some of them, I don't know who exactly." And then Karadzic says: "Please, can you do something about this? I said to him, after what happened in Western Slavonia, we are not going to honour resolutions and contracts ..." You can see this for yourself. I don't have to read it out: "If you shoot, are you going to burn all bridges for future co-operation. We will have to treat you as the enemy. That's what I said on television last night as well. I was pleading. It's not a question of hours, it's a question of minutes. I said that in a few minutes, I cannot even establish contact, let alone do something. I said that I don't even know where these four weapons are." Do you see this entire conversation, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I should just note on the record that I was following the transcript and the exhibit at the same time, and there are quite a few words or phrases or passages omitted in the description of what was in the document. So I just need to put that on the record so when someone reading the transcript turns to the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We have this in evidence, and I take it the general was able to read the passage in its entirety. So what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you see that we were given minutes to do something, and in minutes I cannot even establish contact with my troops? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I announced what was required sometime before the bombing started, and I did it to Mladic and on the television, publicly. I don't know -- I don't recall the time-frame, but it was certainly more than minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since this document was just marked for identification, let's move on to another topic, and then perhaps we can revisit this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did you have the approval of the Bosnian Serbs to bomb their ammunition depots?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just a small clarification. The document was introduced as being a conversation of the 25th of September, according to the transcript. The exhibit indicates the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say the 25th of May, and I mean the first air-strike. You can also read it on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question; approval from the Bosnian Serbs? Was that a question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've moved on to a new topic, the topic of the mandates and the powers of the United Nations forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, the last time we discussed this issue, you agreed that the presence of the UN was there, that the UN was actually present on the ground with the approval of the local authorities, including the Bosnian Serbs. Now, did you have the approval of the Bosnian Serbs for this NATO -- for this air-strike on the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't done on the 1st of May, either. It was the 25th, I think, or 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have a problem with interpretation. I did not say on the 1st of May. Rather, I said the first air-strike in May, at the end of May. Can we briefly see 917 -- 21984, 65 ter. And let me ask you, General, sir, whether at this point in time the United Nations actually stopped being impartial.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I use the phrase something to that effect in this document, if I recall it correctly. The point I'm making is that we've now applied force to one side which -- as a result of the exclusion zone/safe area policy, and we cannot expect or have lost the consent of the Bosnian Serbs. And this is a phrase I think I use in that document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just scroll this up a bit. Let's see point 4(a).

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And let's see what you have to say there: [In English] "UNPROFOR no longer have a peacekeeping relationship with the BSA." The Bosnian Serb Army; right? "(It has lost the consent of one of the parties)."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, that's what I wrote there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "UNPROFOR is very close to being an ally of the Bosnian government (it is very nearly no longer impartial)." In other words, you were fully aware that the Mogadishu line had been crossed?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's for others to decide. I think we're hovering on the edges of it, but that's -- that was my thoughts at that time that night.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this the time for our break or can we go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's time to have a break. How much longer do you have to conclude your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would appreciate it if I can get the entire session, the next session, but I will do my best to complete it sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'll have an hour in the next session. Yes, half an hour, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Muslim side violated provisions on the total exclusion zones; in other words, that it had weapons emplacements that were not at weapons collection points, but, rather, throughout town and in the Marsal Tito Barracks?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they had some weapons outside the weapon collection points; that is to say, weapons that should have been in the weapon collection points that were outside the weapon collection points. I don't think they were in Tito Barracks, but I believe there were some in town that were outside the weapon collection points.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now briefly see 09782 on the 65 ter list. 09782, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this is a telegram sent by Ambassador Akashi to Kofi Annan? And if we now can see paragraph 4, please. The telegram is dated the 26th of May, 1995. Paragraph 4, please. I'd like to refer you to the portion where it says: "General Smith is aware ..." [In English] "... is aware that there are government weapons in Sarajevo that are not in the Tito Barracks or collection point ..." [Interpretation] That's the fourth line from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were NATO air-strikes carried out because of these violations of the total exclusion zones; in other words, were Bosnian Muslims bombed?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have a testimonial to this in P2171, where General Janvier informs Kofi Annan, on the 7th of May, and says that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had five heavy weapons within the total exclusion zone. Can you explain why the Muslim side did not receive the same treatment that the Serbs were put under?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I looking at the 2171 or is that just an extra bit of information?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. This is telegram 09782, and I just quoted another document that was already admitted - that's P2171 - and said that this information about these five weapons was also something that Kofi Annan was informed of therein, and all I want to know is why the Bosnian side was not treated the same way as the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were not using those weapons, as I recall it, at the time. And Akashi says in that telegram that they -- they are in compliance with the warning thus far.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this into evidence, this Akashi telegram to Annan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has it not been admitted yet? Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1051, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take a look at 1D2841, then. 2841, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You will recall, General, sir, that in the first part of your evidence, you said that you were able to observe -- well, actually, you were shown the daily expenditures of weapons, and I would like you now to take a look at this report dated the 31st of May, 1995. The Bosnian Army, the 1st Corps Command, produced this document. This is an interim report, and it discusses the 1st Corps together with special units of MUP, Bosna and Lasta, and it says that they have started with combat actions along such-and-such axis. And could we now just see the part of the document where the ammunition expenditures are shown? Could we see the next page, please. Yes, the next page. General, can you please look at this. It says here that the 1st Corps had 2.055 explosions on that day alone where they were actually opening fire on all Serb lines. So just take a look at the heavy weapons mentioned here: Mortars, 60-millimetre mortars; 90-millimetre rockets. Let's see what else we have here. At the bottom, we can see a 67-millimetre cannon, another 70- and 100-millimetre cannon, and it says: "In the course -- yesterday and today, a large quantity of ammunition was expended, as well as mines and explosives." Even after the warning that was issued, was this mass bombing that was carried out by them, was that something that was -- that went by unobserved?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was unobserved. I'm not sure - I'm pretty certain - that the 60-millimetre mortar wasn't classified as a heavy weapon, and I'm not sure, either, that the 76-millimetre cannon was a heavy weapon either, but there I may be incorrect. The -- and I think the date of this was after we'd stopped bombing, anyhow, because of the hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, perhaps we can take a look at the first page, because I am afraid that there is something that we can't see on this page. It says very clearly there 100 pieces of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Karadzic is reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you were reading too fast so that the interpreters were not able to catch up with you. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Large-calibre explosions mentioned here, we have: TMRKRMT, 500 pieces, bullet; 76 millimetres, P1, 30 pieces; bullets, 76-millimetre ZIS, 30 pieces; 100-millimetre bullet, 30 pieces; 105-millimetre bullet, 30 pieces; 120-millimetre round, 50 pieces; 152-millimetre round or bullet, 20 pieces; 60-millimetre mines, 400 pieces; 82-millimetre mines or shells, 800 pieces; 120-millimetre shells, 150 pieces; 107-millimetre rockets, 15 pieces; and 128-millimetre rockets, 10 pieces, which brings us to a total of 2.055 explosions or detonations on that day, the 30th of May, going on to the 31st. And this report was prepared on the 31st of May. We saw that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 31st.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you know that under the agreement, anything above 20.7 millimetres [as interpreted] was actually prohibited within the total exclusion zone, so anything that went over the 20.7 millimetres [as interpreted]? 12.7-millimetre. The transcript is not correct. 12.7.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- my memory is that that is 12.7 for direct-fire weapons and in excess of 82-millimetre for mortars was the definitions, but that would have to be checked to be certain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think there's -- it's close, Your Honour, but my primary concern is that we moved to the document quickly, and the witness was advised that the document referred to explosions on a particular date, and my recollection, from seeing the document as it moved through, is that it referred to a request for supplemental information. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can read it. With that caveat, shall we admit it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1052, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now briefly see 1D372 [as interpreted], please. 1D3172.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this document. This is a letter sent to General Mladic by you, and on the first page we see the definition of heavy weapons. And then the second bullet point: [In English] "All guns, howitzers and mortars of calibre larger than 12.7 millimetres." [Interpretation] Is that so, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written there. But it's dated, you said, in September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the 4th of September. This is, if I recall the document, me telling Mladic what is to be removed from the Sarajevo exclusion zone after the bombing in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, you did not re-define the 1994 agreement. All you did here was to remind of what the definition of "heavy weapons" was. And if you recall, it was then, too, that everything in excess of 12.7 was mentioned. So this is -- you're just giving a definition here, not a new proposal.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that that's the case at all. I think the situation has changed materially by now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document, please. Before that, can we just see the last page to see that the general signed this letter, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this is your signature?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1053, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, General, that the NATO air-strikes of the ammunitions depot in Pale were not strictly a self-defence move?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't self-defence. They were to reimpose the exclusion zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you were fully aware of the distinction. Can we now briefly see 1D03133. 1D03133. Air-strikes are strategic measures; correct? Here, we see before us a book by Mr. Boutros Boutros-Ghali, the former Secretary-General of the United Nations. Can we now see page 86, please. So on page 86, we can see: [In English] "Air-strikes and close air support was important." [Interpretation] Can we find that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The penultimate paragraph, starting with: "I asked NATO ..." Shall we zoom it further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "I asked NATO to co-ordinate with me ...," and so on. [Interpretation] And then it goes on to say. "... was limited, by resolution, to the protection of UN troops under attack. Air-strikes were a strategic matter, the use of which would signal that the peacekeeping mission had given way to war by NATO and by the United Nations against the targeted forces and their political authorities." [Interpretation] The United Nations -- NATO and the United Nations were actually entering the war -- into war against one side? Was that the case, as stated here by the Secretary-General? Would you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's as he's written it. I think we must be very careful in -- to be clear as to what we mean by the words. Some people use the word "air-strike" to describe any air attack, so if you were flying aeroplanes in close air support, they would carry out an air-strike. In the sense that Boutros-Ghali has used it in this book, he is drawing a distinction between the exclusion zones, and air-strikes. I deduce -- I haven't read the rest of the page to see it, but that's what I understand him to be -- connecting the air-strikes to the exclusion zones, and close air support to the defence of a United Nations -- elements of a United Nations force. And as you see in the document you've already shown me of my own writing in May, I think that we get very close, indeed right on the edges, of our position as peacekeepers when we start to use air-strikes to impose the exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, sir, a moment ago you agreed that the attack on the ammunition depot was not just a matter of defence, but actually an air-strike. And I received the same answer from General Janvier and Ambassador Akashi that these air-strikes were, in fact, a punishment, and we've heard testimony about the same issue by General Rose here. But the point is this is actually moving from confrontation to conflict. Did you, yourself, say that after these air-strikes, you actually crossed the line from confrontation into conflict with one side?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When you're bombing someone, you're in conflict with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You repeated the same things in your conversation with General Mladic on the 28th of May, when you said that there were two types of close air support: [In English] "... as a means of air defence," [B/C/S spoken], "such as the two against the Bosnian Serbs last week ..." [Interpretation] And that you can order either of those types of close air support. Do you recall this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and there were those two types of air-strikes, if you like to call them that. Or let me put it another way. There were two purposes for which you might use air-strikes; one was self-defence and the other one was to do with the imposition of the safe areas and the exclusion zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General, sir, that doesn't apply to the exclusion zones alone, but, rather, to accomplishing objectives that one of the sides is not willing to agree to; in other words, to impose a solution on them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the exclusion zone -- if weapons were being taken out of the weapon collection points or being used to shell the civilian population, then the exclusion zone and safe area decisions were not being carried out, and the -- we then had resource to air-strikes to endeavour to reimpose them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this into evidence, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps the entire document or just that page. I leave it to the Trial Chamber. I don't mean the entire book. I mean the five or six pages that we've used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, what is your observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the operative language is "we've used." I was only aware of, as the Court noted, that particular page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit that page 86. Yes, 86.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1054, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you were determined, in other words, to fight the Bosnian Serbs, correct, and that can explain why it was that the Muslim side was not bombed?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. I was determined to carry out my mandate, which was to see that the safe areas and the exclusion zones were established and maintained. The -- since they were being broken by the Bosnian Serbs, I set about to put them back -- get the situation back to where I wanted it with the means I had available, which included bombing. This I set out to do, and in May this failed to achieve its purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A while ago, we saw which calibre was used by the Muslims to fire at us from these zones, and you didn't punish them for that. Can we now please have Exhibit D1009, page 321.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says in your book: [In English] "My force was composed in the main of battalions from different nations ...," and so on and so on: "As a result, no battalion could be manoeuvred as a whole, which meant the level of the fight I could have was, at the best, that of a reinforced company, subdivision or battalion. However ..." [No interpretation]: "However, the opponent I ultimately came to fight, the Bosnian Serbs, who were operating in company and battalion groups ..." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. So you were fully conscious of the fact that the Serbs were your adversary. This is what is written in your book. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said "ultimately came to fight" or -- yes, I ultimately came to fight. That -- as I've tried to explain, my business was the delivery of aid and the maintenance of the exclusion zones. If I was prevented from doing either of those things, then I had, under certain circumstances, the resource to armed force, and that's what I applied. And since you were preventing me, you got fought. When you stopped, I stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Last time, General, you confirmed that in the first half of 1995 alone, the Muslims launched at least two major offensives from Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- my memory is that they launched one out of Sarajevo, and that was in June. The other two that I confirmed were not out of Sarajevo. One was to the west and the other to the north-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, on that occasion we showed you a document that an offensive started on the 15th of May, and the document just admitted confirms that on the 31st of May, the largest-calibre howitzers, 120-millimetre, 160-millimetre mortars, 100-millimetre guns were used to fire at us from the exclusion zone. Did that hamper your mandate?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a couple of points, Your Honour. I don't think that's a correct representation of what the document states. I made that clarification earlier with respect to whether -- the distinction between firing at a particular time and requests for materiel. And also there seems to be an assumption built into the question about where the forces were located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make the other point that I -- due to your -- Bosnian Serbs' actions, I was in no position to act at all, whatever I wanted to do, on the 31st of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you able to do anything on the 15th of May, before we committed any violations?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you did commit violations, and I seem to recall that my deputy over that period, since I was out of the country, I think, at that time, protested on a number of occasions, and the fighting died down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have records of the consumption from the official Muslim sources. The document referred to by Mr. Tieger said that: "Yesterday and today, the large quantity of ammunition and mines and explosives were consumed by the 1st Corps in Sarajevo." Therefore, there is no doubt that we were under constant attack. So can you tell me who violated the truce? Who violated the Carter Agreement, the Bosnian Serb side or the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I couldn't tell you with any confidence who was the first side to start shooting at each other again after the Carter Agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I wanted to let you know that you have about half an hour to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, but I'm afraid this is really not sufficient. However, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your book, you said -- to be fully effective, let me remind you it's page 348. Can we please have this page on our screens: "To be fully effective ...," and then a little bit further on: [In English] "... there is a need to select targets which will affect the intentions of those one is opposed to, rather than necessarily the specific incidents at hand. To deal with the taking of a bridge in one village, it is sometimes better not to attack the bridge, but to hit a road in another village that is of greater significance to the opponent." [Interpretation] Was this logic of yours the underlying reason for targeting an ammunition depot which was far away from the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that was the first time that the punishment was not effected against the weapon that was in breach, but rather against the side located at a considerable distance?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the -- the effect that I was after was to impress upon the leadership the need to take this decision, and the decision I wanted them to take, which was to remove the weapons from the exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that all those who were involved in air-strikes were combatants?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those carrying out the air-strikes were combatants, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that those who carried out reconnaissance of targets for -- on their behalf behind our lines, and who guided them, as forward air controllers, were also in Pale and that they aided these operations?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No such people existed, as far as I am concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that you didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think any such action was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Didn't you say, yourself, that you posted forward air controllers within the safe zones and that even national contingents had their own forward air controllers that were operating on a compatible basis with NATO?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I did, but there were no forward air controllers involved in the attacks in May.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We don't have any more time for this. We're going to revisit this issue at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, did the Serbs ever give their consent for having these elements, such as scouts and forward air controllers, present in that territory?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you were referring to the forward air controllers that were forward in -- such as those in Srebrenica, I believe you knew that that's what they were -- that's who they were and what they were capable of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
