utterances.text: Sir, let's establish a distinction between the close air support and the attacks. Did we give our approval to have scouts behind our lines who would be party to the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is like asking me as to whether or not I stopped beating my wife, isn't it? Can I have the question phrased so that I can answer it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue: General, you answered that at the time, and we are talking about May, there were no forward air controllers involved in the attacks in May, but there were air controllers, but they were not involved in the attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were forward air control parties in the enclaves. I think it was current Dutch ones in Srebrenica and a -- and, from memory, a British one in Gorazde, but they were not involved in the attacks of May, at the end of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What were they supposed to do? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were there in case they were -- close air support was required in those eastern enclaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did -- the UNPROFOR reports and other intelligence collected on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina were something that were accessible by NATO or were available to NATO?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to differentiate between UNPROFOR reports and other intelligence. UNPROFOR reports were almost certainly copied to NATO. At what level and with what frequency, I cannot recall, but I'm confident it was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were in command of UNPROFOR, did your personnel have access to information on the ground collected by UNMOs, military observers?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I think everyone knows, the UNMOs were not under my command. But at my headquarters, I certainly would see the UNMOs reporting in my headquarters. I don't know how much -- how far down my chain of command those reports went, but I would expect them to go down to the sector headquarters for those operating within that sector. To explain, the Sector Sarajevo would have seen the UNMO reports that concern Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any provision that prohibited your personnel from sharing with NATO what was being received by UNPROFOR? Did you have any such explicit prohibition not to share such things with NATO?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my headquarters, I don't think so. As I said right at the beginning, there was a NATO liaison officer, and I think the general reporting in the headquarters was shared. Now, I can't speak for Zagreb or any other headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that all the captured members of UNPROFOR, captured in May by the Serbs, were active-duty personnel of the United Nations at the time of their capture?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, when did you realise that the Serbs were intent on capturing UN members in the event of an attack in May? Did you know that before the very event took place?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The potential for such an event, yes, I -- that was anticipated. The nature of what happened, no. And I realised it when I was rung up and told that an UNMO would have his throat cut if we didn't stop bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, General, in our meeting of the 9th of May, and this is an exhibit in evidence, your Colonel Baxter said he had intelligence that BiH had begun an offensive to lift the siege of Sarajevo and that he could not allow the UN to help them beat us if NATO was using against the BSA, that our relationship would be -- disappear. Do you remember that if you interfered and called upon NATO to attack us, that that would mean the end of our relationships and that we would become an enemy of yours? If you need reminding, let's look at P2264, paragraph 3. Do you remember this being recorded at this meeting of ours?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to look at the document, please. I don't think Colonel Baxter spoke in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what Mr. Baxter quoted as my words, that I said to you that I had information that an offensive was in the offing and that, in that event, we shall deem you our enemy: [In English] "Our relationship would disappear and we would treat you as the enemy." [Interpretation] In other words, I think it was made very clear to you that if we come under attack, you were no longer going to be our friends and impartial?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we turn the page over, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, I am using too much time on this. This is your minutes of this meeting, and he says: [In English] "He did make a distinction between UNHCR and the ICRC and the UN, who he describes as the armed force of the Security Council." [Interpretation] And it says: [In English] "It is clear the BSA will continue to fight with BiH and that if the NATO are drawn into the fight, the decision has been made to treat UN and NATO as enemies." [Interpretation] This was told you on the 9th of May from the highest place in Republika Srpska, that if you start fighting us, this will turn you into an enemy.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the others, for example, Dr. Zametica and other Serb leaders, inform you, before, during and after the attack, that that was our position? Can we have 65 ter 01343, from which we can see what Dr. Zametica said publicly about this issue. 65 ter 01343: [In English] "A statement made by Dr. Zametica at midnight last night." [Interpretation] That's item C. We need the next page to see item C. It seems we need page 5. Here's the statement made by Dr. Zametica: [In English] "On several occasions ..." [Interpretation] I'll go directly to this portion: [In English] "At meetings here in Pale, we have said to UNPROFOR that should there be any air attacks anywhere in RS, we would treat the entire UNPROFOR, all personnel, as enemies." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says there, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Therefore, there was no doubt that that was the situation; that if we were attacked, we would defend ourselves, and that an attack can only come from an enemy, not from a friend. Do you also know that Dr. Krajisnik said: [In English] "The UN had taken the side of our enemy, and we had to treat the UN accordingly"? [Interpretation] Do you remember him saying that on the 26th of May? It's the same document that I am quoting, and it's on the next page, line 5 or 6 from the top: [In English] "It is incomprehensible ..." [Interpretation] Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "It is incomprehensible that the UN ..." [Interpretation] The last sentence: [In English] "We have the right of defence, and we will use it." [Interpretation] Can we tender this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1055, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have now 1D -- actually, 65 ter 11853.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that at the very outset, the captured men, it was said that they were not hostages, but prisoners of war? Now, you can see Reuters' report of the 1st of June, 1995: [In English] "Karadzic's comment followed warnings to the Western powers." [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please, paragraph 3: [In English] "He said that the detained UN personnel were prisoners of war, not hostages."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Turn on first the microphone. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3: "He said the detained UN personnel were prisoners of war, not hostages." [Interpretation] And the next one: [In English] "... they have to be regarded as prisoners of war because they have the same commander as the one who ordered NATO air-strike." [Interpretation] Were you aware of the fact that our position from the very beginning of bombing was that we were going to consider you as enemy, and that once the bombing started, we were going to capture enemy troops and treat them as prisoners of war? Or to put it simply: Is that consistent with the position that I maintained the whole period?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've got a number of questions there. As I've said to you, and I had heard you at the time, I was well aware that -- that the -- we were vulnerable to having the UN, first of all, being seen as your enemy; secondly, that we would have people taken hostage. Hostages had been taken before, after all. What I saw happen was a number of men being taken hostage, not prisoners of war. I do not consider a prisoner of war is someone who is chained to a gate, or something like that, and having -- with threats that he'd have his throat cut. In my view, that is a hostage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a whole different issue that we will revisit if there is any time left. I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1056, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now briefly see 1D03132. 03132.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an interview that I gave to an Italian news agency from Milan, "Il Giornale," and: [In English] "Why did the Serbs take the blue helmets hostage?" "Karadzic: The UN leaders have turned the blue helmets into an active part of the clash. What is more, Akashi cannot be neutral on the ground and our enemy in the air. I'm talking about the dispatch of fighter bombers." [Interpretation] I speak here about my counterpart, Mr. Akashi, and I say the same things, and I said to him the same things that your counterpart, General Mladic, said to you; is that correct? Was my counterpart Akashi and yours --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could see it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was this, what is stated here on the 23rd of July, consistent with my position on this matter?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably the paragraph in the middle: "Why did the Serbs take the Blue Helmets hostage?" "The UN leaders have turned the Blue Helmets into an active part ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That follows on from your previous statements, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this. And, Your Excellency, I would now urge you to allow me some more time. I would really appreciate that. At least through the end of this session, because I don't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll give you 15 minutes, and please choose the best topics to deal with during that period.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would like to tender this document into evidence and also to add two additional pages from General Smith's book to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Italian news clipping will be admitted as Exhibit D1057, and, of course, the pages 321 and 348 will be added to the book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now move into private session, please, because of the topic that I intend to broach?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, General, that in the fighting around Vrbanja Most on the 27th of May, the UN captured some Serb soldiers that they only released on the 17th of June, when we released the UNPROFOR members?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the date of the release, but I recall at least two Serb soldiers being captured.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly see 1D3231, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true, General, that the deaths occurred when your forces recaptured Vrbanja Bridge from the Serbs? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deaths of whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, were two Serbs killed and four captured at Vrbanja Bridge?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the precise details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, please take a look at your statement, paragraph 128. On the -- [In English] "On the 27th of May, Bosnian Serb troops disguised as French soldiers in UN blue helmets and French uniforms, seized a French position at Vrbanja Bridge in Sarajevo, killing two French soldiers and taking 11 prisoners. The French counter-attacked and recaptured observation post, killing two Serb troops and taking four prisoners." [Interpretation] But this is not how things actually transpired, not in this order. Let's take a look at page 4 here, paragraph 13: [In English] "On 27 May 1995, the Serbs captured an UNPROFOR observation post at the Vrbanja Bridge in Sarajevo, detaining some United Nations soldiers. The position was recaptured by UNPROFOR at the cost of two dead and fourteen wounded. There were also Serb casualties." [Interpretation] In other words, when you recaptured Vrbanja Bridge, you had two deaths and we had two deaths and four wounded; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what you -- you say so. I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We would like to tender this into evidence. This is a cable to the UN. Can we -- we'd like to tender it. This is Akashi reporting to the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1058, perhaps under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we not admit it publicly because we dealt with it in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe you're correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it publicly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, you considered these captured soldiers to be, in fact, prisoners of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose captured soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serb soldiers, Serb soldiers who were captured by your soldiers at Vrbanja Bridge.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave instructions that they were to be treated as prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D01314 -- 013134. And I have to say that I'm under great pressure, in terms of time. 1D01314.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, it should be 1D03134.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3134. 3134, yes, now I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a telegram compiled by you, General?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please see item 4: [In English] "The commanders should be the ones who negotiate ..." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. And then number 5, 5(A). So they are de facto prisoners of war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I put, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "I'm clear in my own mind." So when you capture Serbs, they are prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who are "they" that are referred in this document; the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I am referring to those we have captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, this will be Exhibit D1060.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this one should be under seal, at least temporarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, General, that there were negotiations in order to exchange these men, while we're still in private session?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall negotiations taking place, although I was not part of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I should have said this was Exhibit D1059.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D03135.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a UN document, sir? Please take a look at item 1: [In English] "UN has not the legal right to hold prisoners of war." [Interpretation] And then item 3: [In English] "If UN uses such detainees," and so on, "as bargaining chips ... UN is de facto accepting the rules of the hostage game set by the party." [Interpretation] And then item 4: [In English] "... FMEDO advised that the Serbian soldiers held by UNPROFOR must be released immediately and unconditionally." [Interpretation] Is it correct that the FMEDO advised that they be immediately released?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He may have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this was two days before you wrote that they were, de facto, prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the date -- yes, I think my document -- no, I don't -- was my document the one you had earlier that -- dated the 30th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, right. Then it's two days before.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is an FMEDO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I'm pretty certain this isn't in my headquarters, either. I think this is Zagreb, if only because it's addressed to the force commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1060, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. With respect to "under seal," I don't understand how we can receive documents with no Rule 70 conditions and then they are becoming under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We put it out of an abundance of caution, and we'll deal with it after this has been concluded. We'll revisit all the transcript which was done in the private session and all the documents put under seal. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, you have more? Go until the end of this session. There's only 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, General, sir, that these Serbs were released only when UN members were released, which was on the 18th of June; in other words, that they were exchanged? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to put a few questions to you about Sarajevo. And then, if we have some more time left, I will move on to another topic, one final topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you like to discuss it in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you recall, General, sir, whether the Muslims had ever asked for a cease-fire in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall -- no, I can't recall a case in the time I was commander of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in other areas, they did seek to have a cease-fire in place; in Bihac, Gorazde, and so on?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't immediately recall cases there either, cases in those areas either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any case where we denied a Muslim offer to have a cease-fire in place?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I can't recall the Muslims asking for one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether, while you were there, the Serbs ever launched an offensive in the Sarajevo area with the objective of capturing a Muslim portion of the town?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my time there, I don't -- I can recall attacks, but not -- not in such a size and scale that they appeared to be wanting to take territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that we declared unilateral cease-fires on occasions of some religious holidays, but also outside of that, in Sarajevo, itself? That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have occurred. I don't remember them in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed that they launched offensives. Do you remember, General, that Muslims took advantage and exploited the NATO air-strikes carried out in 1995, both in May and later on?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not take advantage, in my memory, at all. They did not take advantage in May. In September, or late August and September, they did not take advantage of the air-strikes in the vicinity of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see 1D3222, please, in e-court. And just can we admit -- or has this previous document been admitted already? All right, very well. We have these two maps under the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, can you see here that the borders, HVO borders, and the BH Army lines of October 1995 have been marked on this map, and can you agree with me that the Serbs thereby lost a significant part of the territory?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Zoom in to the legend so the general can see that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can see where the VRS was and how it withdrew?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is over by Bihac, isn't it? My memory of the map --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's in South-Western Bosnia, between Jajce and Donji Vakuf. At Vlasic, as it were. Thank you. Can we see the next page, please. Can you see, General, that this is to the south of Sarajevo, and it depicts the same period, October 1995, or, rather, January through October 1995, showing how Serb forces lost these villages at the foot of Bjelasnica, which had been in our hands and then we handed them over to UNPROFOR, and would you agree with me that this constitutes loss of territory?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd certainly agree that the map shows that the Bosnian Serbs moved further east, the -- and lost the ground that they were holding at the beginning of the year. In the period, moved further east by October 1995, that's what the map shows. The -- yes, that's what the map shows.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender this document, these two pages, the two maps. Perhaps they can be admitted as one exhibit or two, whatever you choose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we heard about the origin of this map, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was trying to refresh my recollection about that earlier. I can't bring it to mind, but if it's -- whatever the origin, I gather it wasn't previously admitted, and I certainly don't see anything about the question and answer, that is eliciting this witness's map-reading skills, that would give rise to admission.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can assist. When we showed the first map in this series, it was clear that it was a map -- a CIA map, and we identified them then. And I believe that one of those maps has been admitted, showing the offensive and counter-offensive near Bihac, and I believe this was a map depicting 1994. We used it with General Rose's testimony, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, could you agree that what is depicted on this map reflects the situation at the time; i.e., you said that Bosnian Serbs moved further east and lost the ground that they were holding at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In broad terms, I -- that happened by the end of October. I wouldn't want to be any more precise than that. And that would apply to both of those maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And with that, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1061, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now it's really time for you to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two quick documents. D929, D929, just to show you, General, a report of the 29th of May, the UN report, and to show that the UN was aware that the Muslim side was taking advantage of the situation. Can we see the last page, "Assessment," please, or, rather, the penultimate page, before last. Can we see where it says "A4"? Is that bottom of the page, it says "A4." These are tables and addresses that we see here. Here we have it now: [In English] "Assessment: The ABiH are taking advantage of the BSA preoccupation with the UN and NATO to mount offensives in the Komusina and Ozren Salient. It is thought that most of their assets are likely to be committed to these offensives, but future action with an objective of Donji Vakuf cannot be ruled out."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it clear to the UN then that elsewhere in Bosnia, the Muslim side was taking advantage of the situation and exploiting the outcome of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear that that's the assessment of the headquarters of this document, which I think is Sector South-West by the units that are in it -- that are mentioned in it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And one final document, 65 ter 02278, please. While we wait for it to come up, I have to say that we haven't even touched on the issue of weapons smuggling and many other areas, such as the abuse of the situation around the airport and several other topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have a Serbian version before me. This is a document from the 28th Division, and that's a military unit of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Srebrenica. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems so, yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the course of the Muslim offensive in Sarajevo, we see what the 8th Division was doing here. It was deployed in Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, and: "... although facing big problems in connection with food supplies and protecting the area," and so forth, "... decided to contribute to the fight against the aggressor, and, with that aim, have intensified their activities deep inside the territory temporarily occupied by the aggressor. In the course of their combat operations, reconnaissance and sabotage groups and the 28th Division encountered several times the enemy." And so on. And then you can see what they did. They executed 13 Serbs or killed 13 Serbs, seized so and so, and then it says that: "In order to prevent enemy forces from sending additional forces from the Srebrenica and Zepa area to the Sarajevo theatre ..." And then it says what the outcome was, seven people captured, and so on and so forth. So, sir, can you see here that 10 days before the Serbs captured Srebrenica, they were killing Serb forces and stretching them across the lines in order to prevent them to go to Sarajevo? So does this show that there was an increase of activities in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say it was an increase, but it certainly reports the activities they were carrying out as at the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1062, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Last question, General. Should one look specifically where a shell fell to see whether there is a particular target there in order to be able to characterise that shell?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it important for you and your people to know fully what the deployment of the opposing forces was in your zone? Was it not important for you to know deployment, as a whole, of personnel and equipment?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of all the parties, do you mean, or just me, my forces? Of course, I wanted to know where mine were, and I tried to know where both the Bosnian Serbs and the Federation forces were and what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did either side succeed in concealing anything before you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, General, sir. My apologies for this rush, and, therefore, some of my questions were unclear because I was not systematic enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you have some re-examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour. We'll resume at five past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to begin with a question that was raised, I believe, last Thursday at pages 11468 through 1169 [sic]. General, at that time you were asked about the information you received, whether you saw things for yourself or had certain services that sent you information. The question was: "How was it that you received information ...," et cetera. And you indicated that in most cases, you were relying on reports from subordinates and occasionally went to see something yourself. I'd like to explore with you, a bit further, the breadth and consistency of the information which you received about political and military events and incidents in your area of responsibility. First of all, did you receive daily reports from various sources, both civil and military, in the UN chain of command?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was a reporting system that I was part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were briefings held on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a morning brief which, if I was in my -- if it was in Sarajevo, I attended, and in the afternoon I would meet again with, sort of, my principal staff officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the morning briefing include not only members of your staff, but also representatives from other agencies present in Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, such as UNHCR were there, and the sector headquarters would send a liaison officer up and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you also receive information from the journalistic community which was present in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not -- they didn't report to me, in a sense, but one -- my spokesmen were in touch with them continuously, and I had the practice of meeting, usually over dinner, certain journalists during a week or when there was the opportunity occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to these sources, did you also have contact with representatives of both the Bosnian Government and the Bosnian Serb authorities at both the political and military level?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as has just been discussed during this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I believe you indicated earlier there was, for example, a liaison officer at Lukavica from the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A Major Indic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I wanted to turn next to a document that the accused showed you at page 11 -- or beginning at page 11512. That was P906. This was a document which he asserted was a telegram sent at 10.36 on the 29th of August from Janvier. And if we could call that document up, please. Mr. Karadzic then referred to your third phone call with General Mladic during that period on 29 August, at 10.00 a.m., during which you told Mladic that it had been established beyond reasonable doubt that the shell that killed over 30 persons and injured more than 80 others had been fired from Bosnian Serb-held territory. And then the accused said to you, at page 11513: "So at 10.00, you inform Mladic that it is beyond any reasonable doubt, and your commander, General Janvier, 40 minutes after you, says that that is not the case, that it was not established, that it cannot be established?" And that was on the basis of this document, P906. Now, can I ask you, General, to look at P906, and tell us if, in fact, it is a UNPF daily sitrep which covers the time-period for 28 August 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It covers the period 28 -- the day of the 28th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that it emanates from G-3 and not from General Janvier at all? I think we see the drafter --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The drafter is the staff officer, grade 3 of operations. He has signed it as the releasing officer, and he's sending it to a very large stream of people, including UN headquarters, in the name of Lieutenant General Janvier. In other words, this is a routine reporting process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it correct, therefore, General Smith, that this is not a determination by General Janvier that what you were telling Mladic on the 29th of August was not correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a day -- this is a comment of a day before the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Staying on that theme for a moment, I want to turn your attention to questions that were asked regarding your conclusions concerning Markale II at page 11515. Mr. Karadzic pointed you to language in a document, indicating that the Cymbeline radar was operating, and if the rounds were fired close to the confrontation line, they would have been detected, and if fired from a longer range, the arc of the trajectory would "most likely" have been below the beam of the Cymbeline radar, thus not detected. And focusing on that language, "most likely," he asked you: "What does that sound like to you? Does it sound like reasonable doubt?" Now, and you indicated, in response, that: "While not an absolute positive, it is most likely to be positive." Let me ask you about your conclusions, General, a little bit further. First of all, you told the Court, at pages 11457 through 58, that in addition to the UNMO and Sector Sarajevo reports, you brought into your judgement all the other systems; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, simply that -- if your determination that the rounds had been fired by the Bosnian Serbs was based on a single factor or, instead, on a weight of the combination of the factors put together?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was a combination of the factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did that include, for example, the fact that no one heard a round fired from within the proximity of Sarajevo, although, as you testified --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid this is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, he referred to the reason given by the witness. Hear him out. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, did that include the fact that no one heard a round fired from within the proximity of Sarajevo, despite the sound that a mortar makes and despite the presence of military personnel listening for such incidents?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a factor in this judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, you were asked at pages 11547 and 548 about the alleged probability of hitting the particular spot where the Markale II shell landed, and you said, at page 11548, that you didn't see why this alleged fact should have been brought to your attention, since the civilian areas of Sarajevo were "a substantial target" and "much wider than nine metres wide." So, General, let me ask you directly. Did that mean that you considered that it was the civilian areas of Sarajevo, generally, that were targeted by the Bosnian Serb Army and not just the specific spot where the shells ultimately landed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. You know, these questions really are leading. That suggests an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I can see why you might think that, Mr. Robinson, but I think, in reality, it's a question which is designed to elicit a more particular answer by the witness, which is a perfectly valid tactic in re-examination, to which the answer is not fixed. It can be answered in the positive or the negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, do you have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just re-reading the question. The point I was trying to make there was that it was a civilian target that had been hit, and the -- and it was civilians in the market that had been killed and wounded. It wasn't that particular spot that was the target and had been the result of this attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about another discussion that the accused raised with you concerning shelling. At pages 11544 through 45, there was -- there were some questions about shelling and a discussion about alleged prohibitions of fire on the city. You responded that, in fact, fire was coming into the city. And then the accused asserted: "That was the case only when we were being shot at. Returning fire is legitimate." So, General, I wanted to ask you a few follow-up questions in connection with that. First, during the course of your service in Sarajevo, was there Bosnian Serb fire on the city that was unrelated, insofar as you and your staff could tell, to any outgoing fire; that is, fire from the Bosnian Serbs that took place when they had not been fired on?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were occasions when one couldn't see, as it were, the cause for that effect, and there were other occasions where there were no military targets, as such, where the rounds were falling, but you might have been able to connect them as a cause and effect because of some incident on the line of confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, was there also fire from the Bosnian Serbs into the city that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the Prosecutor is draining the witness in order to make him give him the answer that he did not give and that he would like to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not the one who raised the issue of legitimate fire. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you reformulate the question, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you testified that there was fire after -- after -- let me see if I can reformulate that. Right. You indicated that there was sometimes fire from the Bosnian Serbs after they had been fired on, but into areas where there were no military targets. Was there also fire, after the Bosnian Serbs had been fired on, into the city that failed to discriminate between possible military targets and civilian areas?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- I find that question hard to answer from my memory, but if -- nevertheless, from my memory, if there was a military target and there was some -- some fire fell close to that military target and on the civil population, then that would have been understood as part of the same military engagement. It was when rounds fell in a civil area, where we had no indication or knowledge of any military target that we could see there, that we would understand that as being an attack directly onto a civil -- the civil areas of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, you were asked some questions about the NIOD report at a couple of junctures during your cross-examination, including pages 11670 and then, in particular, at page 11728. And, Your Honour, if we could have just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you some follow-up questions about that. First of all, generally, was -- when you were -- you spoke with the NIOD people, is this some kind of personal dissertation on your part or were you asked questions to which you were asked to respond?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this was some time ago, I think about 10 years ago now, and they came to my office in the headquarters I was in. And I think they had sent a sort of questionnaire in advance of -- not so much the specific questions, but the sort of area in which questions would be asked, if I remember correctly. And we then -- there was then an interview with, I recall, fairly long answers, in that these were mostly scene-setting type of questions. I'd long -- I've only seen the document they produced once or twice before seeing it here again. And the content of that interview was then reduced, if you like, to the -- to the sort of thing you saw produced in court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You said it was scene-setting. Was it, in part, aimed at attempting to get information on how events might have been prevented?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really remember. It was -- my understanding of what they were trying to do was to understand what had happened and the setting of -- in which it had happened so as to understand why it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at page 11728, the accused cited the report to show efforts by internationals, or a passage from that report attributed to you, to show efforts by internationals to create a rift in the Pale leadership and decrease his influence. And as noted in at page 11727 in his question, to reduce his influence over Mladic is how he put it. And this is an issue that came up again today. And, incidentally, I wanted to ask you: To the extent that you were aware of any efforts by international figures to isolate Mr. Karadzic, did you understand that to be because of some personal dislike or because they understood or considered him to be in control of events they wanted to change?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of the isolation was nothing to do with the events of day-to-day life in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The isolation was that it was thought possible to make a deal with Milosevic, who had more -- perhaps more at stake and was -- therefore, leverage and so forth could be brought to bear upon him in a way that wasn't going to be possible or didn't appear to be possible with Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe, in fact, you were asked at 11728, or you were pointed to that part of the report that said: "Had Mladic been Milosevic's man, Srebrenica would not have happened." And when you were asked to explain that, you said: "Milosevic would have understood the setting of the Srebrenica and the no-fly zones and the exclusion zones in a different way to the Bosnian Serbs." That was at 11729. And I take it you recall that.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, earlier in your testimony, you had referred to the -- at page 11354, the isolation or unworldliness of Mr. Karadzic at points, views that were not based on a world that anyone else was sharing, and that was at 11674 through 75, and to a meeting with Mladic in August, trying, without success, to explain to him that the Bosnian Serb perception of the world was to their disadvantage. Do you recall those? That was at 11449. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when you referred in your answer concerning the comment in the NIOD report, that is, Milosevic would understand it in a way different to the Bosnian Serbs, which Bosnian Serbs were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to Dr. Karadzic, who -- and the people around him in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just so the Court understands this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Tieger. Did you say that Mladic would understand it in a different -- in a way different to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. If I said that, I meant "Milosevic," and I hope I was understood that way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And going back to the previous question: Had Mladic been Milosevic's man, Srebrenica would not have happened, I think your answer, cited by Mr. Tieger, was given to my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you mean that it was Mr. Karadzic that -- because of Karadzic, Srebrenica -- what happened in Srebrenica happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. What I'm saying is, and I think that's what I was saying to the investigation by the Dutch, was that Milosevic had an understanding or appeared to me to have had an understanding of what was going on around him, and he would have seen the potential of dangers of allowing the pocket of Srebrenica to fall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And by "Srebrenica," did you mean the taking of a safe enclave or the massacre that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't -- I can't remember which bit of that or whether I was saying it about the whole. I just don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just in follow-up to the President's question: Did that mean, General, that you were saying that it was only Milosevic who could have influenced Mladic because he had a particular view or perhaps a more realistic view, in your judgement, and Karadzic and Mladic were coming at it from the same perspective?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. That is a leading question. Perhaps even Judge Morrison could agree with me on that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Mr. Robinson. I think on this occasion, that is certainly a leading question, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, this is a difficult one to parse out, Your Honour, but I'll be happy to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What's the connection between your observations that it might have been different if Mladic had been Milosevic's man and the fact that Karadzic and Mladic were the Bosnian Serbs who saw things differently from Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm sorry. You're bordering on inviting speculation, and I think we're going down a very dangerous route here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you were asked quite a number of questions about attacks from the enclaves, that is, from Srebrenica, most recently today, in fact. And I believe at one point, in response to a question by the accused - that would be 11682 -- he asked you to agree with him that the attack on Srebrenica was a reaction to attacks from the enclaves, and you said: "I think that was the immediate cause, yes." I wanted to ask you about less immediate causes, both ones you may have indicated in your testimony and others. First of all, General, you explained what has come to be known as your thesis to the Court, and I believe you indicated that - and that's contained in both your amalgamated statement and your testimony - that you concluded that the Bosnian Serbs were determined to resolve, by military operations, in order -- the issue of Srebrenica in order to alleviate over-stretching of manpower required by the need to guard the enclaves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- in the thesis, they were -- it wasn't just Srebrenica. They were going to resolve this whole affair militarily, and the -- and to do that, they needed to squeeze the enclaves. The -- and that was to reduce their significance in their rear area and free up the resources that were currently committed to that -- to guarding that threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you arrived at this conclusion at a fairly early stage in your tenure in Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometime in early March, this -- after the visit where I met -- Srebrenica, where I had met General Mladic at Vlasenica afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I presume that your -- you arrived at this conclusion without benefit of access, for example, to internal Bosnian Serb military records or contemporaneous internal political documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm losing track of who's testifying here. These last two questions is just Mr. Tieger testifying and asking leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think you are beginning to behave a little bit like Dr. Karadzic in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but with respect to the previous answer, I thought it was -- while arguably leading, it was a predicate question about which there was no dispute. But, fine, I will ask it in a classically non-leading way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General Smith, in arriving at your thesis, did you have access to internal Bosnian Serb military records or to internal political documents?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did your thesis, as you've explained it to us, about squeezing the enclaves and why that would -- why the Bosnian Serbs would undertake that effort, preclude the possibility that there might be other factors that underpinned or supported an intention to squeeze or move on the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was wide open to other information coming in. This was the intention. The purpose of the thesis is to guide my own analysis and understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to now direct your attention to a few documents that, principally Bosnian Serb military documents, and then ask you a question or two about that. First, if we could call up P00976. This is a document dated 19 November 1992. It's a directive for further operations of the Army of Republika Srpska, and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this from 1992? Would that be right for that witness? I'm wondering.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The issue has been raised by the accused, Your Honour, of -- or the position taken by the accused is that the actions taken against the enclaves, and in particular Srebrenica, was a purely reactive, one, two attacks out of the enclave in 1995, in particular. You've heard the general identify his conclusion that well before that action was taken, he arrived at the conclusion that such action would be taken, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without having to hear further explanation, let us see whether the general is able to answer any question about the document which originates from 1992. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm going to just show you a couple of documents very quickly, and read from them quickly. This is a document signed by General Mladic. Part of it states: "From its present positions, the main forces --" this is for the Drina Corps, "Its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad, the dam, Zvornik and the corridor, while the rest of its forces --" And this is on page 5 of the English, at the bottom. "... while the rest of its forces in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, and force him to leave the Birac, Zepa and Gorazde areas together with the Muslim population." Now, General, 65 ter 2085 is a document dated 24 November 1992. It's a decision for further operations to the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade pursuant to the document we just saw, the directive to the Main Staff, and in part one it indicates: "... launch an attack using the main body of troops and major equipment to inflict on the enemy the highest possible losses, exhaust them, break them up, or force them to surrender, and force the Muslim local population to abandon the area of Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I say, before an answer is given: I keep saying that this document has been mistranslated. Mladic is not saying that they should surrender. He's saying that they should disarm. And Mladic also is saying that since the people are going, that they should take the army as well; that it's not that the people should go with the army, it's the other way around. I have cautioned against this translation, and now this witness is going to be put in a difficult position because he's supposed to respond on the basis of a poor translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are referring to Directive 4, not this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What is this? I don't know what this document is, but he showed Directive 4 and he quoted, I mean Mr. Tieger did, that they should surrender. But Mladic is saying that they should disarm and become civilians. And, secondly, Mladic did not say that the army should lead the people; rather, the people should take the army along, as that is what is happening anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, the witness must have heard your interpretation or reading. Let's carry on, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I am not going to take you through the whole panoply of documents which this Court will see during the course of the case. What I simply wanted to ask you, if these are among or the types of documents that might have further informed your thesis and expanded your view of the reasons why the Bosnian Serb political and military forces might move on the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just -- before I answer, could I just see -- you've got this daily report up here, but I couldn't find the bit you were quoting from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree. I'm sorry, I didn't see that that one was up there, because the one to which I referred, I believe, was 65 ter 2085. Perhaps I misspoke or perhaps my number is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was -- this document was here, but can I just say one word. Again, we are on the wrong path. Directive 4 does not talk about the ground. It is "4/1" and its executive, and it says something different. Directive 4/1 is the relevant document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The confusion, Your Honour, was that it actually is an exhibit, not a 65 ter number. So it is 2085, but P2085.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You refer to Exhibit P2085, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- this one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this of -- that I've now got on the screen is also 1992, and it's part of the cascade of orders, as I understand it, of -- that stems from the original directive you showed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, and I believe I've drawn your attention to paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My question was, simply, without going through a long list of documents, whether these are among the kinds of documents that would have further informed your thesis and expanded your understanding of why the Bosnian Serb political and military forces could be expected to move on the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. If he didn't see these documents, I don't understand how this question helps the Chamber if this isn't the kind of documents that would have informed his thesis then. I simply don't understand what is being asked General Smith and how it would assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or could it be asked whether it is consistent with his thesis?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I had to reverse engineer my thesis, I would have to write something like that at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Thank you, Mr. President. Just I wanted to ask you a couple of questions about convoy restrictions, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There were many questions posed to you concerning the -- concerning restrictions, and I believe it was posed to you that restrictions that were imposed on humanitarian aid and UN resupply convoys were due to a concern about supplying Bosnian forces in the enclaves. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to look at a couple of documents in that connection. First, 65 ter 3675. This is a document from the Main Staff in April of 1995. And if we turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the Serbian version as well, because the translations are a disaster.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, it may be a bit difficult to read the English when it's that size, but I'll do my best to point to you it. The remark is: "We did not approve the following:" And it identifies, in the second paragraph below that -- well, first, in the first paragraph, "Swedish construction project," and then in the paragraph below that: "In addition to the above, we did not approve beef, salt, oil and clapboards for the enclave ..." And, similarly, I wanted to turn your attention to 65 ter 03673. This is also a Main Staff document, Main Staff of the VRS, from April 1995, to the Commands of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and Drina Corps, advising them that they have not approved the following UNPROFOR convoys and teams. If we look, for example, to item 4: "A convoy which was supposed to transport 12 containers with humanitarian aid (beds, food, clothes, medicines and school supplies)." And if we look to item 10, the last page, page 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Can we see all of page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The rejection of a convoy to Srebrenica which was supposed to transport various goods; a water trailer, a large quantity of field beds, hospital beds, an X-ray machine, beams for construction, nails, light fittings, a satellite telephone system and cables, signalling equipment, roofing material, et cetera. And cleaning goods, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I wanted to ask you: Are these documents consistent with your understanding at the time of -- and consistent with your thesis about the intention to squeeze the enclaves and consistent with your understanding at the time about why humanitarian and UN resupply convoys were restricted?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those remind me, you know, that that was going on, and -- and the extensive nature of what was being -- of the convoys we were -- we weren't able to move. And, yes, it fitted with the thesis. It was -- it reinforced that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Your Honour, I tender those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those two will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 03675 was admitted as Exhibit P839, and 65 ter 03673 will be Exhibit P2309.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the number of the first one?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first 65 ter number was 03675, which was admitted as Exhibit P839.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is already admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please be given the possibility to point out just one document and put two brief questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll consider it at the end of direct examination. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That does conclude my redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before putting your question, tell us what the question is about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first question is whether, in 1992, there were any safe areas. That's the first question, whether the general knows whether safe areas existed. The second question has to do about the time of Markale, the document of the Norwegian Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we allow you to put those questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D3219, could we have that, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that: General, do you know that safe areas were established only in 1993, in the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- I did know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger asked you about what was going on during the war in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, he showed me a document of that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please now focus on this document. Do we agree that this is a document that covers the 28th and 29th of August, and on the 29th of August, at 1800 hours, it was sent -- the Norwegian Battalion sent it to their own country? 29th, at 1800 hours, August 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it, date, time, group.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, Sarajevo Sector. And I would like everyone to look at the whole passage, and I'm going to read only one sentence: [In English] "It has not been confirmed where the shells came from either."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Therefore, not even at the end of the day on the 29th, the Norwegian Battalion was able to determine from which direction the fire came and to put it in the report that they are sending to their government?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't. This is a battalion up in the Tuzla area, and it would seem to me they are sending a situation report of the whole area back to their government. And what they're working from is other people's reports from the other sectors that have been copied to them. That's what I think is happening, but you'd need to get the -- someone from the Norwegian Battalion to explain the process for certain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the same time, they have information that the church at Ilidza, and we know it was an Orthodox Church, that was hit, and that at least one person died from the wedding party at the time. Can we have this document admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The last bit was an unnecessary statement. Yes, we can admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1063, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Chamber, and thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, Sir Rupert. I thank you, on behalf of the Tribunal and the Bench, for your coming yet again to the Tribunal to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Is the next witness ready? I was told so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we often work over time, could we adjourn for the day, because I find it difficult to switch from one witness to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We're ready to go. It's Dr. Karadzic's cross-examination. The witness is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I hope at least we can hear the examination-in-chief, at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is the continuation of a witness whose cross-examination began yesterday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I was carried away. I'm sorry. He was waiting all the time, yes, Mr. Glavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Glavas. Please make yourself comfortable. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I apologise for your inconvenience, for the delay. Although we have only 25 minutes, we'll continue with your cross-examination. If you're ready, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Glavas.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Forgive me in advance if I sometimes address you as General Smith, because we just finished with him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that yesterday, we stopped at a point when certain activities were rounded up in which the Muslim side finalised some of its activities relating to the increase of number of reserve police officers and providing weapons for them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In an interview with my adviser, you said that prior to the outbreak of the conflict, the large part of the Muslim population had been evacuated. Can you explain how this happened, and were there any Serbs crossing over from one zone to another?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I spoke about similar things when I talked to representatives of the OTP both in Sarajevo and here in The Hague. Therefore, the fact is that after certain organisational activities were finalised pursuant to the directive issued by the then Crisis Staff of the Bosnian side, the composition of which we had at the time, although I am reluctant to give you the names now, although I know them, therefore, according to the directive issued by this Crisis Staff, the population from the area of Ivancica and Zivici [phoen] were nearly all evacuated towards Romanija. The village of Dupovci, which is on the very entrance point of Hadzici, was evacuated towards Gradac and Pazaric, and one part of Zunovnica and Binjezevo neighbourhood were evacuated in the direction of Mount Igman. Based on the intelligence gathered on the ground, we knew for certain that that was a predetermined and designed move by the Bosnian authorities, which they saw as the way of dealing more easily with the remaining minority Serb population in Hadzici. In the meantime, and that's common knowledge, they arrested all able-bodied Serbian men between Zovik and Gornja Rastovica, they arrested them, put them in detention, and confiscated their weapons. And I used to say that that was a classical example of a military strategy, to -- such strategy, to ensure they are rear lines. They also attacked the village of Bradina, which was populated exclusively by Serbs, and they practically saw this as an obstacle because they perceived that as a buffer zone between the territory under their control and the territory towards Konjic. So they arrested the population there, including, as I said, the Serbs, arrested in Hadzici from Lazovi [phoen] to Gornja Rastovica, and thereby completed the preparations. And then around the 25th of May, they carried out an all-out attack on Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In order to assist the Chamber and all the other parties, can we please now have 1D674. 1D674, and I would kindly ask you to mark these places that you just mentioned. So can we have 1D674 in e-court, please. Thank you. This is an ethnic map of Sarajevo. Can you mark, for the benefit of the Chamber, the location of Hadzici municipality?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This map is not something we got notified on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can lead with proceeding with this map. ^

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I see, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have three maps. I think that this one is the clearest one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that Hadzici is to the south-west, somewhere near this area which is marked with number 7?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is Hadzici, where a Serbian majority lived, and what is this on the left? These green areas signify Muslim villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please circle the Serbian villages which are within the Muslim territory?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I find it very difficult to find my bearings in the map. In reality, I can orientate myself excellently, but I'm not sure how you will also find your way around this map vis-a-vis these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may help you, Mr. Glavas. Blue are Serbian villages, yellow is one Croatian village, and Muslim villages are painted green. Now, from number 7, if you go up and to the left, you can see a few Serbian villages, and then we also see Tarcin, Pazaric, and the remaining Muslim villages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you telling me that the Serbs from these villages that were in the Muslim territory were arrested?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I'm sorry. Now, from the very beginning of the war, a line was established from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the place names slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Glavas, the interpreter couldn't hear the names of the places. Could you repeat your answer, kindly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, no problem. So at the beginning, there was a sort of improvised separation line from Tinovo elevation to Dupovci and to the maintenance centre, all the way up towards Mostar. Now, from Gornja Rastovica to the tunnel was the territory that was absolutely under the control of the Bosnian Government, both then and throughout the entire war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about evacuation of the Muslim civilians from this Serbian zone, were you referring to these green villages that were within the red circle?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you put the number 1 next to the first circle? Am I right if I say that you have encircled the town of Hadzici and the surrounding Serbian-held territories?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR GLAVAS [Resumed]
